solution:
**a - 3, b - 4, c - 2, d - 1.**

| Group 'A' | Group 'B' | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\) (ethane) | 3. Saturated hydrocarbon | All valencies are satisfied by single bonds. The chapter says "Ethane & propane are saturated hydrocarbons." |
| b. \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\) (ethyne) | 4. Triple bond | The two carbon atoms are joined by three covalent bonds; the chapter calls such hydrocarbons 'Alkynes'. |
| c. \(\text{CH}_4\text{O}\) (methanol) | 2. Molecular formula of an alcohol | Table 9.17(b) lists Methanol, molecular formula \(\text{CH}_4\text{O}\), condensed structural formula \(\text{CH}_3-\text{OH}\), as the first member of the homologous series of alcohols. |
| d. \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\) (propene) | 1. Unsaturated hydrocarbon | Table 9.15 lists Propene \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\) in the "Unsaturated hydrocarbons" column: it contains a carbon-carbon double bond. |

**Methane, \(\text{CH}_4\).**

Carbon has the electronic configuration 2, 4 — that is, 4 electrons in its valence shell; each hydrogen atom has 1 electron in its K shell.

The carbon atom is written in the centre with one hydrogen atom to its left, one to its right, one above and one below. Between the carbon and EACH hydrogen a pair of electrons is shown (one electron contributed by carbon, shown as a dot, and one contributed by that hydrogen, shown as a cross). Each such shared pair is one covalent bond, so four single covalent bonds are formed:

\(\text{H} : \text{C} : \text{H}\) — with a further \(\text{H}\) joined by a shared pair above the carbon and another below it.

All four of carbon's valence electrons are used in bonding, so **carbon carries no unshared (lone) pair**. Counting the four shared pairs, carbon is surrounded by 8 electrons and so attains the configuration of neon; each hydrogen is surrounded by 2 electrons and attains the configuration of helium.

The corresponding line structure (structural formula) is \(\text{CH}_4\) drawn as a central C joined by four single lines to four H atoms.

[Textbook note: this molecule's electron-dot structure is drawn in the chapter as Fig. 9.11, but that figure is captioned "Electron-dot structures of **ethane**". The structure drawn there is ethene, not ethane — it shows only four hydrogen atoms and two shared pairs between the carbons, and it appears at the end of the Step 1-3 derivation of ethene \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_4)\) beside Fig. 9.10. Ethane \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_6)\) has its own, different electron-dot structure at Fig. 9.9 on the previous page. The caption should read "ethene".]

**Ethene, \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\).**

Each carbon atom has 4 valence electrons and each hydrogen has 1. Following the chapter's own three steps: join the two carbon atoms, attach the 4 hydrogen atoms (two to each carbon), and then find that one valency of each carbon is still unsatisfied — so a **double bond** is drawn between the two carbon atoms in place of the single bond.

In the electron-dot structure the two carbon atoms are written side by side with **two shared pairs (four electrons) between them**, and each carbon shares one pair with each of its two hydrogen atoms:

\(\text{H}_2\text{C} :: \text{CH}_2\)

Each carbon spends 2 of its 4 valence electrons on its two C-H bonds and the remaining 2 on the carbon-carbon double bond, so **no lone pairs remain on either carbon**. Each carbon is surrounded by 8 electrons and each hydrogen by 2.

The line structure is \(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2\).

**Methanol, \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\).**

Carbon has 4 valence electrons, oxygen has 6 (configuration 2, 6) and each hydrogen has 1.

- The carbon atom shares one electron pair with each of **three** hydrogen atoms — three C-H covalent bonds.
- The carbon atom shares its fourth electron pair with the **oxygen** atom — one C-O covalent bond.
- The oxygen atom shares one more electron pair with the **fourth** hydrogen atom — one O-H covalent bond.

\(\text{H}_3\text{C} : \text{O} : \text{H}\)

Oxygen uses only 2 of its 6 valence electrons in these two bonds, so the remaining 4 are shown as **two unshared (lone) pairs of dots on the oxygen atom** — the chapter notes that it is essential to show all the valence electrons in an electron-dot structure. Carbon carries no lone pair.

Counting shared and unshared electrons, carbon and oxygen are each surrounded by 8 electrons and each hydrogen by 2.

The line structure is \(\text{CH}_3-\text{O}-\text{H}\), i.e. \(\text{CH}_3-\text{OH}\), the first member of the homologous series of alcohols.

**Water, \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\).**

Oxygen has the electronic configuration 2, 6 — that is, 6 electrons in its valence shell; each hydrogen has 1.

The oxygen atom is written in the centre with one hydrogen on either side. Oxygen shares **one electron pair with each hydrogen atom** — two O-H single covalent bonds. Following the chapter's own instruction for this molecule, the electrons of the oxygen atom are shown as dots and those of the hydrogen atoms as crosses:

\(\text{H} : \text{O} : \text{H}\)

Oxygen uses only 2 of its 6 valence electrons in bonding, so the other 4 are shown as **two unshared (lone) pairs of dots on the oxygen atom**, one above it and one below it. Oxygen is thus surrounded by 8 electrons (attaining the neon configuration) and each hydrogen by 2 (attaining the helium configuration).

The line structure is \(\text{H}-\text{O}-\text{H}\).

**\(\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\) has only ONE structural formula — propane.**

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\)

Drawn in full, the three carbon atoms are joined in a straight chain by single bonds, and the eight hydrogen atoms satisfy the remaining valencies — three on each end carbon and two on the middle carbon.

**There is no isomer.** A branched chain needs a carbon atom attached to a side chain, and with only three carbon atoms any attempt to draw a "branch" simply gives the same straight chain of three carbons drawn in a bent way. Branching first becomes possible at four carbon atoms, which is why the chapter introduces structural isomerism with \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\) and not with propane. Table 9.12 accordingly lists \(\text{C}-\text{C}-\text{C}\), propane, as a straight chain hydrocarbon.

**\(\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\) has TWO structural formulae.** This is the chapter's own example of structural isomerism (Fig. 9.13).

**(i) A straight chain of four carbon atoms — n-butane:**

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\)

**(ii) A branched chain — isobutane (i-butane):** three carbon atoms in a chain with the fourth carbon attached as a branch to the middle carbon.

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_3\)

Both have the same molecular formula \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\) but different structural formulae, so they are two different compounds. The chapter names this phenomenon **structural isomerism**, and calls the two compounds n-butane (normal-butane) and i-butane (iso-butane). Table 9.15 lists isobutane \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\) as its example of a branched chain saturated hydrocarbon.

**\(\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\).** The chapter itself names one compound of this molecular formula — **propyne** — in Table 9.15, where Propyne \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\) is the straight-chain unsaturated example. It also fits the general formula the chapter gives for alkynes, \(\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n-2}\), with \(n = 3\).

**(i) Propyne** — a triple bond between the first two carbon atoms:

\(\text{CH} \equiv \text{C}-\text{CH}_3\)

Two further structures are possible on the chapter's own rules — that two carbon atoms may be joined by one, two or three covalent bonds, and that carbon chains may be open or closed (rings):

**(ii) Propadiene** — two double bonds sharing the middle carbon:

\(\text{CH}_2=\text{C}=\text{CH}_2\)

**(iii) Cyclopropene** — a closed chain (ring) of three carbon atoms carrying one double bond, with two hydrogen atoms on the saturated carbon and one on each of the doubly-bonded carbons.

In each case the four hydrogen atoms exactly satisfy the valencies left over after the carbon skeleton is drawn. Note that the chapter names only propyne; structures (ii) and (iii) follow from the chapter's statements about multiple bonds and about ring structures such as cyclohexane and cyclohexene, but are not themselves named anywhere in the chapter.

**Structural isomerism** is, in the chapter's own words, "the phenomenon in which compounds having different structural formulae have the same molecular formula".

The compounds concerned are different compounds — they have different structural formulae and therefore different properties — even though counting their atoms gives the same molecular formula.

**Example:** the molecular formula \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\) corresponds to two different structural formulae (Fig. 9.13):

- a straight chain of four carbon atoms, \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\), called n-butane; and
- a branched chain, \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_3\), called isobutane.

The chapter notes that the number of carbon compounds increases further because of the isomerism observed in carbon compounds — it lists isomerism as one of the four characteristics of carbon responsible for the very large number of carbon compounds.

**A covalent bond** is, in the chapter's own words, "the chemical bond formed by sharing of two valence electrons between the two atoms".

Carbon has 4 electrons in its valence shell. It cannot reach a noble gas configuration by losing all four (the resulting \(\text{C}^{4+}\) would be unstable — small in size with a high net charge) or by gaining four (the resulting \(\text{C}^{4-}\) would be equally unstable). It therefore attains the neon configuration by **sharing** its four valence electrons with the valence electrons of other atoms. Both atoms then attain a noble gas configuration without any net charge being generated on them, so both remain electrically neutral and both gain stability.

One pair of shared electrons constitutes one covalent bond. A covalent bond is also represented by a small line joining the symbols of the two atoms — this line structure is also called the structural formula.

**Example:** in the hydrogen molecule (Fig. 9.3), two hydrogen atoms each share one electron; the resulting shared pair is a single covalent bond, \(\text{H} : \text{H}\), written as \(\text{H}-\text{H}\). In methane, \(\text{CH}_4\), the carbon atom forms four such covalent bonds, one with each hydrogen atom.

**A hetero atom** is, in the chapter's own words, "the atom of the element which is substitute for hydrogen" in a hydrocarbon chain.

Many carbon compounds are formed when carbon bonds with elements other than hydrogen — the chapter names **halogens, oxygen, nitrogen and sulphur**. Atoms of these elements substitute one or more hydrogen atoms in the hydrocarbon chain, and in doing so the tetravalency of carbon is still satisfied. Sometimes the hetero atoms are not alone but occur as part of a group of atoms.

A compound acquires specific chemical properties because of its hetero atom, irrespective of the length and nature of the carbon chain in that compound.

**Example:** in chloroethane, \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl}\), the chlorine atom has taken the place of one hydrogen atom of ethane, so chlorine is the hetero atom. Likewise the oxygen atom in ethanol, \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}\), and the nitrogen atom in methanamine, \(\text{CH}_3-\text{NH}_2\), are hetero atoms.

**Functional groups** are, in the chapter's own words, "these hetero atoms or the groups of atoms containing hetero atoms" — the part of a carbon compound that gives it its specific chemical properties, irrespective of the length and nature of the carbon chain in that compound.

The chapter adds that the **carbon-carbon double and triple bonds are also recognised as functional groups**, because the compounds containing them get specific chemical properties due to them. In a structural formula the free valency of a functional group is shown by a short line; the functional group takes the place of a hydrogen atom and is joined to the carbon chain by that valency.

**Example:** the alcohol group \(-\text{OH}\) is the functional group of ethanol, \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}\). Table 9.16 lists the functional groups the chapter deals with: halo \(-\text{X}\), alcohol \(-\text{OH}\), aldehyde \(-\text{CHO}\), ketone \(-\text{CO}-\), carboxylic acid \(-\text{COOH}\), ether \(-\text{O}-\), ester \(-\text{COO}-\) and amine \(-\text{NH}_2\).

Because the chemical properties come from the functional group and not from the chain length, all the compounds \(\text{CH}_3-\text{OH}\), \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}\), \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}\) behave very similarly.

**Alkanes** are the saturated hydrocarbons. The chapter states it directly: from the structural formulae of ethane and propane it is seen that the valencies of all the atoms are satisfied by **single bonds**; such compounds are called saturated compounds, and "Saturated hydrocarbons are also called 'Alkanes'."

So an alkane is a compound of carbon and hydrogen only, in which every carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen bond is a single covalent bond and the tetravalency of every carbon atom is satisfied without any double or triple bond.

The chapter gives the general molecular formula of the homologous series of alkanes as \(\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}\).

**Examples:** methane \(\text{CH}_4\), ethane \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\) (\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_3\)), propane \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\) (\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\)) and butane \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\) — the first members of the homologous series of alkanes listed in Table 9.17(a). Because the single bonds C-H and C-C are very strong, the chapter notes that saturated hydrocarbons are not reactive and remain inert in the presence of most reagents.

**Unsaturated hydrocarbons** are, in the chapter's own words, the carbon compounds "having a double bond or triple bond between two carbon atoms" — restricted to hydrocarbons, that is, compounds containing carbon and hydrogen as the only two elements.

The chapter divides them into two kinds:

- the unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a carbon-carbon **double** bond are called **alkenes**;
- the unsaturated hydrocarbons whose structures contain a carbon-carbon **triple** bond are called **alkynes**.

**Examples:** ethene, \(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2\) (\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\)), an alkene; and ethyne, \(\text{CH} \equiv \text{CH}\) (\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\)), an alkyne. Table 9.15 adds propene \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\) and propyne \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\).

The chapter also notes two consequences: unsaturated compounds are generally **more reactive** than saturated compounds and undergo addition reactions, and they burn with a yellow sooty flame because the proportion of carbon in them is larger.

**A homopolymer** is a polymer formed by the repetition of a **single** monomer. The chapter puts it exactly so: of the polymers listed in Table 9.27 it says "The polymers in the above examples are formed by repetition of single monomer. These are called homopolymers."

A polymer is a macromolecule formed by regular repetition of a small unit, and that small repeating unit is the monomer; so in a homopolymer every repeating unit is of one and the same kind.

**Example:** **polyethylene**, formed by the polymerisation of a single monomer, ethylene \(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2\) (Fig. 9.26); it is used for carry bags and sports wear. Other homopolymers listed in Table 9.27 are polystyrene (from styrene), polyvinyl chloride (from vinyl chloride), polyacrylonitrile (from acrylonitrile), teflon (from tetrafluoroethylene) and polypropylene (from propylene).

The chapter contrasts these with **copolymers**, which are formed from two or more monomers — its example is PET, polyethylene terephthalate.

**A monomer** is, in the chapter's own words, "the small unit that repeats regularly to form a polymer".

The chapter defines the pair together: a macromolecule formed by regular repetition of a small unit is called a polymer, the small unit that repeats regularly to form that polymer is called the monomer, and the reaction by which monomer molecules are converted into a polymer is called **polymerisation**.

**Example:** ethylene, \(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2\), is the monomer of polyethylene (Fig. 9.26). One important method of polymerisation named in the chapter is exactly this — making a polymer by joining alkene-type monomers.

Table 9.27 gives further examples: styrene \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\) is the monomer of polystyrene, vinyl chloride \(\text{Cl}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\) of PVC, and propylene \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\) of polypropylene. Natural polymers have monomers too: Table 9.28 gives glucose as the monomer of cellulose, alpha amino acids of proteins and isoprene of rubber.

[Textbook note: this chapter does not define the term "reduction" anywhere. Its "Chemical Properties of Carbon Compounds" section names only four reaction types — combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution — and the words "reduction" and "reduce" do not occur in the chapter outside this exercise item. The answer below is therefore built from the reaction the chapter DOES teach that is a reduction, namely the addition of hydrogen to an unsaturated compound, which the chapter presents as an addition reaction and never calls a reduction.]

**Reduction** is the converse of oxidation. The chapter defines oxidation in terms of oxygen — it calls oxidants "substances that can give oxygen to other substances" — so on the chapter's own terms the reverse change is the **addition of hydrogen to a compound, or the removal of oxygen from it**.

**Example from this chapter — hydrogenation.** An unsaturated compound undergoes an addition reaction with hydrogen to form a saturated compound, for which a catalyst such as platinum or nickel is necessary:

\(-\text{C}=\text{C}- + \text{H}_2 \xrightarrow{\ \text{Pt/Ni}\ } -\text{CH}-\text{CH}-\)

The chapter's own application of this reaction is the **hydrogenation of vegetable oils in the presence of a nickel catalyst**: the molecules of vegetable oil contain long unsaturated carbon chains, hydrogenation transforms them into saturated chains, and Vanaspati ghee is thereby formed.

**Oxidants** are, in the chapter's own words, "substances that can give oxygen to other substances"; they are also called **oxidising agents**.

The chapter introduces them by contrast with combustion: when a carbon compound burns in air, all the chemical bonds in its molecule break and \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) are formed, so the compound is completely oxidised. But chemical compounds can also be used as a source of oxygen, and an oxidising agent acts on certain functional groups present in carbon compounds rather than destroying the whole molecule.

The chapter names **potassium permanganate** and **potassium dichromate** as the oxidising agents commonly used.

**Example:** alkaline potassium permanganate oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid —

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\ \text{alkaline KMnO}_4\ } \text{CH}_3-\text{COOH}\)

Only certain bonds in the vicinity of the functional group take part in this reaction. In the chapter's activity, the pink colour of the potassium permanganate added to warm ethanol disappears at first because the permanganate is being used up in the oxidation; once all the ethanol has been oxidised the excess permanganate is no longer used up and its pink colour stays.

**Butane.**

The structural formula \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\) contains **four** carbon atoms in a straight chain and no functional group — every valency is satisfied by single bonds.

By Step 1 of the chapter's IUPAC method, the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms is the parent alkane, and the alkane with four carbon atoms is **butane** (Table 9.12). There is no functional group, so no suffix or prefix is added (Step 2), and no numbering is needed (Step 3).

IUPAC name: **butane**.

**Propan-2-ol.**

Step 1: the chain \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CHOH}-\text{CH}_3\) has **three** carbon atoms, so the parent alkane is **propane**.

Step 2: the functional group is the alcohol group \(-\text{OH}\), whose condensed name is **ol**; the last letter 'e' of the parent name is replaced by it, giving **propanol**.

Step 3: the carbon carrying the \(-\text{OH}\) group is the **middle** carbon. Numbering from either end gives it the number 2, so both numberings are equivalent and the locant is 2. A digit and a letter are separated by a small horizontal line.

IUPAC name: **propan-2-ol**.

This is the chapter's own first worked example in Table 9.20, where it is shown with both numberings marked equivalent.

(Its common name is isopropyl alcohol; the chapter does not give it.)

**Propanoic acid.**

Step 1: the chain \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}\) has **three** carbon atoms — note that the carbon of the \(-\text{COOH}\) group is counted — so the parent alkane is **propane**.

Step 2: the functional group is the carboxylic acid group \(-\text{COOH}\), whose condensed name is **oic acid**; replacing the last letter 'e' of "propane" gives **propanoic acid**.

Step 3: the chapter's rule is that the number 1 is assigned to the carbon in the functional group \(-\text{CHO}\) or \(-\text{COOH}\) when one is present. Here that is fixed automatically and no locant needs to be written in the name.

IUPAC name: **propanoic acid**.

Compare Table 9.19, where \(\text{CH}_3-\text{COOH}\) (two carbons) is named ethanoic acid by the same steps.

**Ethanamine.**

Step 1: the chain \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{NH}_2\) has **two** carbon atoms, so the parent alkane is **ethane**.

Step 2: the functional group is the amine group \(-\text{NH}_2\), whose condensed name is **amine**; replacing the last letter 'e' of "ethane" gives **ethanamine**.

Step 3: the chapter notes that numbering is usually not required if the carbon chain contains only two carbon atoms.

IUPAC name: **ethanamine**.

Compare Table 9.19, where \(\text{CH}_3-\text{NH}_2\) (one carbon) is named methanamine by the same steps; Table 9.21 gives the common name of the present compound as ethyl amine.

**Ethanal.**

Step 1: the structural formula \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CHO}\) has **two** carbon atoms — the carbon of the \(-\text{CHO}\) group is counted — so the parent alkane is **ethane**.

Step 2: the functional group is the aldehyde group \(-\text{CHO}\), whose condensed name is **al**; replacing the last letter 'e' of "ethane" gives **ethanal**.

Step 3: the chapter's rule assigns the number 1 to the carbon of the \(-\text{CHO}\) group, and in any case numbering is not required for a chain of only two carbon atoms.

IUPAC name: **ethanal**.

Compare Table 9.19, where \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CHO}\) (three carbons) is named propanal; Table 9.21 gives the common name of the present compound as acetaldehyde.

**Butan-2-one.**

Step 1: the chain \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\) has **four** carbon atoms, so the parent alkane is **butane**.

Step 2: the functional group is the ketone group \(-\text{CO}-\), whose condensed name is **one**; replacing the last letter 'e' of "butane" gives **butanone**.

Step 3: the chain can be numbered from either end. Numbering from the left puts the carbonyl carbon at position 2; numbering from the right puts it at position 3. The chapter's rule is to accept the numbering that gives the **smaller** number to the carbon carrying the functional group, so the locant is 2.

IUPAC name: **butan-2-one**.

The book itself writes this compound simply as "butanone" in Q7(h) of this same exercise — the two names refer to the same compound, since a four-carbon ketone can only have its carbonyl group at position 2. Table 9.21 gives its common name as ethyl methyl ketone.

**Oxidation.**

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}\)

An **alcohol** (propan-1-ol) is converted into a **carboxylic acid** (propanoic acid). Comparing the two, the compound has gained oxygen: the \(-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}\) group has become a \(-\text{COOH}\) group.

This is exactly the reaction the chapter treats under its heading "2. Oxidation", where ethanol is oxidised by alkaline potassium permanganate to ethanoic acid:

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\ \text{alkaline KMnO}_4\ } \text{CH}_3-\text{COOH}\)

The chapter notes that in such a reaction only certain bonds in the vicinity of the functional group take part — unlike combustion, in which all the chemical bonds in the molecule break.

[Textbook note: the equation is printed in the book without oxygen on the left-hand side and is therefore not balanced as it stands. The complete combustion of propane is \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 + 5\ \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 3\ \text{CO}_2 + 4\ \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{heat} + \text{light}\). The question asks only for the type of the reaction, which the printed products already settle; the chapter itself sets the balanced propane equation as a "Use your brain power" question.]

**Combustion.**

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow 3\ \text{CO}_2 + 4\ \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

A hydrocarbon (propane) is burnt to give **carbon dioxide and water** as the products. The chapter's first chemical property is exactly this: "Hydrocarbons as well as most of the carbon compounds undergo combustion in presence of oxygen to emit heat and light and form carbon dioxide and water as the common products." Its own worked examples are \(\text{CH}_4 + 2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{heat} + \text{light}\) and the corresponding reaction of ethanol.

**Addition reaction.**

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{CHBr}-\text{CHBr}-\text{CH}_3\)

The chapter's definition fits exactly: "When a carbon compound combines with another compound to form a product that contain all the atoms in both the reactants, it is called an addition reaction." Here every atom of the unsaturated hydrocarbon and both bromine atoms appear in the single product.

The reactant is an **unsaturated** compound — it contains a carbon-carbon double bond, which the chapter treats as its functional group. The double bond is used up in the reaction and the product is **saturated**, one bromine atom having added to each of the two carbon atoms that carried the double bond.

The chapter adds that this addition takes place instantaneously at room temperature and that the accompanying disappearance of the bromine colour can be seen by eye, which is why the reaction is used as a **test for the detection of a multiple bond** in a carbon compound.

**Substitution reaction.**

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_3 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl} + \text{HCl}\)

The chapter's definition fits exactly: "The reaction in which the place of one type of atom / group in a reactant is taken by another atom / group of atoms, is called substitution reaction." Here one hydrogen atom of ethane has been replaced by a chlorine atom, and the displaced hydrogen leaves as hydrogen chloride.

The reactant is a **saturated** hydrocarbon. The chapter explains that because the single bonds C-H and C-C are very strong, saturated hydrocarbons are not reactive and remain inert in the presence of most reagents — but that in the presence of **sunlight** they react rapidly with chlorine, the chlorine atoms replacing the hydrogen atoms one by one. Its worked example is the chlorination of methane, which gives four products in succession: \(\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}\), \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\), \(\text{CHCl}_3\) and \(\text{CCl}_4\).

**Dehydration reaction.**

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

One molecule of **water is removed** from the alcohol, and the unsaturated compound left behind carries a carbon-carbon double bond where the \(-\text{OH}\) group and a neighbouring hydrogen atom used to be.

The chapter treats this reaction under the heading "(ii) Dehydration reaction", among the chemical properties of ethanol: "When ethanol is heated at the temperature \(170\ ^\circ\text{C}\) with excess amount of concentrated sulphuric acid, one molecule of water is removed from its molecule to form ethene, an unsaturated compound."

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\ \text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4,\ 170\ ^\circ\text{C}\ } \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Here the concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a **dehydrating agent**. The chapter itself sets the corresponding question for n-butyl alcohol — the very compound in this item — as a "Use your brain power" exercise.

**Neutralisation reaction** (the reaction of a carboxylic acid with a strong base).

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

An acid and a base react to give a **salt and water**. The chapter states this under the chemical properties of ethanoic acid: "Ethanoic acid gives neutralization reaction with a strong base sodium hydroxide to form a salt and water", with the worked example

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{COOH} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{COONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

labelled Acid + Base gives Salt + Water. The chapter notes that the reactions of a carboxylic acid are mainly due to its \(-\text{COOH}\) functional group, and that the IUPAC name of the salt formed in its own example is sodium ethanoate (common name sodium acetate). By the same naming, the salt formed here is sodium propanoate.

**Esterification reaction.**

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3-\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{COO}-\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

A **carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol** to give an ester and water. The chapter states the rule under its heading "ii. Esterification Reaction": "Substances having ester as the functional group are formed by reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol", and gives the worked example

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\ \text{acid catalyst}\ } \text{CH}_3-\text{COO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

in which ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of an acid catalyst to form the ester ethyl ethanoate. In the present item the alcohol is methanol instead of ethanol, so the ester formed is methyl ethanoate.

The chapter adds that esters have a sweet odour, that the odour of most fruits is due to an ester present in them, and that esters are used for making fragrances and flavouring agents.

**Pentan-2-one:** \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\)

Reading the name backwards through the chapter's steps: the suffix **one** is the condensed name of the ketone group \(-\text{CO}-\); the parent **pentan(e)** means a chain of **five** carbon atoms; and the locant **2** places the carbonyl group on the second carbon of that chain.

Drawn in full, the second carbon is the carbonyl carbon: it carries an oxygen atom joined to it by a **double bond** written above it, and its other two valencies go to the \(\text{CH}_3-\) group on one side and the \(-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\) chain on the other.

This is the chapter's own third worked example in Table 9.20, where the same structural formula is numbered from both ends and named pentan-2-one.

**2-Chlorobutane:** \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CHCl}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\)

The parent **butane** means a chain of **four** carbon atoms. The chapter notes that the condensed name of the halogen functional group is always attached as a **prefix**, not a suffix — so **chloro** is written in front, and the parent name keeps its final 'e'. The locant **2** places the chlorine atom on the second carbon of the chain.

Drawn in full, the second carbon carries one hydrogen atom and one chlorine atom, and the tetravalency of every carbon atom is satisfied.

Compare Table 9.20, whose second worked example is 2-chloropentane, \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CHCl}-\text{CH}_3\) numbered so that the chlorine gets the smaller number.

**Propan-2-ol:** \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CHOH}-\text{CH}_3\)

The suffix **ol** is the condensed name of the alcohol group \(-\text{OH}\); the parent **propan(e)** means a chain of **three** carbon atoms; and the locant **2** places the \(-\text{OH}\) group on the second — that is, the middle — carbon.

Drawn in full, the middle carbon carries one hydrogen atom and one \(-\text{OH}\) group.

This is the chapter's own first worked example in Table 9.20, where it is noted that numbering this chain from either end gives the \(-\text{OH}\) group the number 2, so both numberings are equivalent.

**Methanal:** \(\text{HCHO}\)

The suffix **al** is the condensed name of the aldehyde group \(-\text{CHO}\), and the parent **methan(e)** means a chain of **one** carbon atom.

The single carbon atom of the molecule is therefore the carbon of the \(-\text{CHO}\) group itself. Its four valencies are satisfied by a double bond to the oxygen atom and single bonds to two hydrogen atoms, so the structural formula is

\(\text{H}-\text{CHO}\), that is, \(\text{HCHO}\), with the C and O joined by a double bond.

(Its common name is formaldehyde; the chapter does not give it. Compare Table 9.19, where the two-carbon and three-carbon members of the same homologous series are ethanal \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CHO}\) and propanal \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CHO}\).)

**Butanoic acid:** \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}\)

The suffix **oic acid** is the condensed name of the carboxylic acid group \(-\text{COOH}\), and the parent **butan(e)** means a chain of **four** carbon atoms — of which the carbon of the \(-\text{COOH}\) group is one.

So three \(-\text{CH}_2-\) / \(\text{CH}_3-\) carbons precede the \(-\text{COOH}\) group. No locant is needed, because the chapter's Step 3 assigns the number 1 to the carbon of the \(-\text{COOH}\) group whenever one is present.

Compare Table 9.19, where \(\text{CH}_3-\text{COOH}\) (two carbons) is ethanoic acid by the same reasoning.

**1-Bromopropane:** \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{Br}\)

The parent **propane** means a chain of **three** carbon atoms. As the chapter notes, the condensed name of a halogen functional group is always attached as a **prefix**, so **bromo** is written in front and the parent name keeps its final 'e'. The locant **1** places the bromine atom on the first — that is, an end — carbon of the chain.

The same molecule may equally be written \(\text{Br}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\); compare Table 9.19, which writes bromoethane as \(\text{Br}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\).

(Table 9.21 lists the corresponding chlorine compound under the common name n-propyl chloride.)

**Ethanamine:** \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{NH}_2\)

The suffix **amine** is the condensed name of the amine group \(-\text{NH}_2\), whose hetero atom is nitrogen, and the parent **ethan(e)** means a chain of **two** carbon atoms.

No locant is needed — the chapter notes that numbering is usually not required if the carbon chain contains only two carbon atoms.

Compare Table 9.19, where the one-carbon member of the same series, \(\text{CH}_3-\text{NH}_2\), is named methanamine. Table 9.21 lists the present compound under the common name ethyl amine.

**Butanone:** \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\)

The suffix **one** is the condensed name of the ketone group \(-\text{CO}-\), and the parent **butan(e)** means a chain of **four** carbon atoms. The carbonyl carbon carries a doubly-bonded oxygen atom.

No locant is printed in the name and none is needed: in a four-carbon chain the ketone group cannot be on an end carbon (an end carbon carrying a doubly-bonded oxygen would be an aldehyde, \(-\text{CHO}\)), and numbering from either end then gives the same compound. Written out with its locant the name is butan-2-one, which is how the same compound is asked about in Q5(f) of this exercise.

Table 9.21 lists this compound under the common name ethyl methyl ketone.

The chapter gives **four characteristics of carbon** that together account for the very large number of carbon compounds — it notes that about 10 million carbon compounds are known, a number larger than the total number of compounds formed by all the other elements put together.

**a. Catenation.** Carbon has a unique ability to form strong covalent bonds with other carbon atoms, which results in the formation of big molecules. The bond between two carbon atoms is strong and therefore stable. The chains so formed may be **open chains** — either straight or branched — or **closed chains**, that is, rings.

**b. Multiple bonds.** Two carbon atoms can be bonded together by one, two or three covalent bonds — a single, double or triple bond. The chapter's example is that three different compounds containing two carbon atoms exist for this reason: ethane \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_3\), ethene \(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2\) and ethyne \(\text{CH} \equiv \text{CH}\).

**c. Tetravalency.** Being tetravalent, one carbon atom can form bonds with four other atoms — carbon or otherwise — and the compounds differ in their properties according to the atoms bonded to the carbon. The chapter's example is the five compounds formed from one carbon atom with hydrogen and chlorine: \(\text{CH}_4\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}\), \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\), \(\text{CHCl}_3\) and \(\text{CCl}_4\). Carbon similarly bonds with O, N, S, halogens and P.

**d. Isomerism.** Compounds having different structural formulae can share the same molecular formula, which increases the number of carbon compounds still further.

Table 9.15 of the chapter classifies hydrocarbons into **three types by the shape of the carbon skeleton**, each of which may be saturated or unsaturated. The saturated members of the three types are:

**1. Straight chain hydrocarbons** — the carbon atoms are joined one next to the other in a single unbranched chain.
Example: **propane**, \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\), that is \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\).

**2. Branched chain hydrocarbons** — the chain carries a side chain, so at least one carbon atom is bonded to more than two other carbon atoms.
Example: **isobutane**, \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\), that is \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_3\).

**3. Cyclic hydrocarbons** — the carbon atoms form a closed chain, that is, a ring.
Example: **cyclohexane**, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\), a ring of six carbon atoms (the chapter also gives cyclopentane, \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\)).

All three are saturated because in each of them the valencies of all the atoms are satisfied by single bonds, which is the chapter's definition of a saturated compound.

Table 9.16 of the chapter lists **six** functional groups whose hetero atom is oxygen — alcohol, aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid, ether and ester. Any four, with the name and structural formula of one example of each:

| Functional group | Condensed formula | Example (name) | Example (structural formula) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Alcohol | \(-\text{OH}\) | Ethanol | \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}\) |
| 2. Aldehyde | \(-\text{CHO}\) | Ethanal | \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CHO}\) |
| 3. Ketone | \(-\text{CO}-\) | Propanone | \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_3\) |
| 4. Carboxylic acid | \(-\text{COOH}\) | Ethanoic acid | \(\text{CH}_3-\text{COOH}\) |

In the aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid and ester groups the oxygen atom is joined to the carbon atom by a **double bond**; in the alcohol and ether groups it is joined by single bonds only.

The two remaining oxygen-containing groups, had they been chosen instead, are the **ether** group \(-\text{O}-\) and the **ester** group \(-\text{COO}-\); the chapter's own example of an ester is ethyl ethanoate, \(\text{CH}_3-\text{COO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\).

Table 9.16 of the chapter lists exactly **three hetero atoms** — halogen, oxygen and nitrogen. One functional group from each, with the name and structural formula of one example:

| Hetero atom | Functional group | Condensed formula | Example (name) | Example (structural formula) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Halogen (chlorine) | Halo (chloro) | \(-\text{Cl}\) | Chloroethane | \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl}\) |
| 2. Oxygen | Alcohol | \(-\text{OH}\) | Ethanol | \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}\) |
| 3. Nitrogen | Amine | \(-\text{NH}_2\) | Methanamine | \(\text{CH}_3-\text{NH}_2\) |

Each of these is a hetero atom in the chapter's sense: an atom of an element other than hydrogen that has substituted a hydrogen atom of the hydrocarbon chain, while the tetravalency of carbon remains satisfied. The compound acquires its specific chemical properties from that group, irrespective of the length and nature of its carbon chain.

Any oxygen-containing group from Table 9.16 (aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid, ether or ester) could stand in place of the alcohol group, and bromine or iodine in place of chlorine.

Table 9.28 of the chapter, "Some natural polymers and their occurrence", gives the following. Any three:

| Natural polymer | Place of occurrence | Monomer |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Cellulose | Wood (cell walls of plant cells) | Glucose |
| 2. Proteins | Muscles, hair, enzymes, skin, egg | Alpha amino acids |
| 3. Rubber | Latex of the rubber tree | Isoprene |

The chapter's table also lists **polysaccharide** (monomer glucose, occurring as starch), **D.N.A.** (monomer nucleotide, deoxyribose-phosphate, occurring in the chromosomes of organisms) and **R.N.A.** (monomer nucleotide, ribose-phosphate, occurring in the nucleus and cytoplasm of the cell), any of which could be given instead.

The chapter describes polysaccharides, proteins and nucleic acids as "the supporting pillars of the living world" — we get food, clothing and shelter from the polysaccharides starch and cellulose; proteins constitute a large part of the bodies of animals and are responsible for their movement and various physiological processes; and nucleic acids control heredity at the molecular level. Rubber is named as another type of natural macromolecule.

**Vinegar.** The chapter states that vinegar is a **5-8 % aqueous solution of acetic acid** (ethanoic acid). Its use, in the chapter's own words, is as a **preservative in pickles**.

Ethanoic acid itself is a colourless liquid boiling at \(118\ ^\circ\text{C}\); its aqueous solution is acidic and turns blue litmus red. (The chapter adds that pure ethanoic acid melts at \(17\ ^\circ\text{C}\), so in cold countries it freezes at room temperature and looks like ice — hence the name glacial acetic acid.)

**Gasohol.** The chapter explains it in the science box "Alcohol : A fuel". When molasses, obtained during the production of sugar from sugarcane, is subjected to **fermentation**, alcohol (ethanol) is obtained. On combustion in sufficient air ethanol gives carbon dioxide and water as the only products, so it is a **clean fuel**. It is therefore used in some countries as an **additive to increase the efficiency of petrol**, and such a fuel is called **gasohol**.

**A catalyst** is, in the chapter's own words, "such a substance due to presence of which rate of reaction changes without causing any disturbance to it" — that is, the substance alters the rate of the reaction while itself remaining unchanged by it.

**A reaction brought about by the use of a catalyst — hydrogenation.** An unsaturated compound can undergo an addition reaction with hydrogen to form a saturated compound, but the chapter notes that "it is necessary to use a catalyst like platinum or nickel for this reaction":

\(-\text{C}=\text{C}- + \text{H}_2 \xrightarrow{\ \text{Pt/Ni}\ } -\text{CH}-\text{CH}-\)

The chapter's own application of it is the **hydrogenation of vegetable oils in the presence of a nickel catalyst**: the molecules of vegetable oil contain long unsaturated carbon chains, and hydrogenation transforms them into saturated chains, forming Vanaspati ghee.

A second example from the chapter is the **esterification** reaction, in which ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of an **acid catalyst** to give ethyl ethanoate and water.
